author: EmuCore - Hub
title: mGBA rescales cached DMA offsets when GBA audio forces 32-bit FIFO transfers
summary: A FIFO DMA can be programmed at 16-bit width, then converted to 32-bit transfers by the GBA audio path. mGBA now rescales the cached source step to plus or minus four bytes, preserving direction and preventing doubled or misaligned sample reads.
heroAlt: Close-up of the Game Boy Advance audio circuitry on its motherboard.

blocks.text: The game’s DMA width is cached early

mGBA records source and destination offsets when the GBA writes the DMA control register. A game can configure that channel for 16-bit transfers, which gives the cached source step a two-byte stride. The audio FIFO later uses the same DMA mechanism but imposes its own transfer width, so the earlier setting must be reconciled with the new use.
FIFO audio changes the transfer width

When mGBA schedules FIFO DMA, it forces the channel to 32-bit width and a fixed destination. Before this correction, it cleared the destination offset but retained the cached source offset from the original 16-bit setting. The engine then advanced two bytes while consuming four-byte audio words, duplicating and misaligning portions of the sample stream.
Rescale the source step and keep its sign

The merged fix normalizes a positive source offset to `4` and a negative offset to `-4` after the width is forced to 32-bit. Zero remains zero. Preserving the sign keeps the source-control direction intact while aligning subsequent reads to the width the FIFO transfer now uses. The destination continues to use the fixed FIFO address.
The regression was isolated by bisection

The pull request documents a bisect using Classic NES Series: The Legend of Zelda and a repeatable hard-jump oracle. It identified the earlier cached-offset refactor as the regression boundary. That gives developers a concrete playback case for checking that FIFO samples no longer combine doubled or misaligned bytes across repeated DMA requests.
